passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel cognitive training program on working memory performance in adults aged 25–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups: (1) the training group received 30 minutes of adaptive working‑memory tasks daily for four weeks; (2) an active control group completed 30 minutes of non‑adaptive memory tasks; and (3) a passive control group received no intervention. Pre‑ and post‑tests measured reaction times (RT) on a digit‑span task. The study aimed to determine whether the adaptive training would produce measurable improvements in RT compared to controls and to assess the magnitude of any effect. Table 1 reports post‑test values. The researchers hypothesized that the training group would show a statistically significant reduction in mean RT relative to both control groups, with the active control exhibiting a modest improvement due to general task engagement. The study’s implications could inform educational and clinical interventions targeting working‑memory deficits.
stem: Which group exhibited the lowest mean reaction time after the intervention?

options.D: All groups had identical mean RTs

explanation: The table shows the Training group’s mean RT (420 ms) is lower than both control groups (460 ms and 470 ms), indicating faster responses.
trap: Treating a higher reaction time as better performance; a lower RT means faster responses, and Training's 420 ms is the lowest mean.

stem: Which experimental design feature best controls for potential confounding variables in this study?

options.B: Using a passive control group only
options.C: Collecting data at a single time point
options.D: Blinding participants to the study purpose

explanation: Random assignment distributes individual differences evenly across groups, reducing confounding. The passive control alone would not control for placebo or engagement effects, and single‑time‑point data would not allow pre‑post comparisons.
trap: Choosing participant blinding, which the passage never describes and which addresses only expectancy, not the pre-existing differences that random assignment balances.

stem: What is the percent reduction in mean RT for the Training group relative to the Passive Control group?
explanation: Correct: A) (470 − 420)/470 × 100 = 50/470 × 100 ≈ 10.6%. Why the others are wrong: B) 4.3% (20/470) does not match the 50 ms difference. C) 11.9% divides the 50 ms difference by the Training mean (420) instead of the Passive Control reference. D) 2.1% (10/470) is the Active versus Passive Control difference.
trap: Dividing the 50 ms difference by the Training mean (420 ms), which gives 11.9%, instead of by the Passive Control reference (470 ms).

stem: Which group has the highest standard deviation in reaction time?

options.D: Both Active Control and Passive Control equally

explanation: The table lists SDs of 35 ms (Training), 40 ms (Active Control), and 45 ms (Passive Control). The Passive Control group has the highest SD.
trap: Confusing variability with the mean or assuming the two control groups tie; the SDs are 35, 40 and 45 ms, so only the Passive Control has the highest.

stem: Which comparison in Table 1 best isolates the benefit of the adaptive nature of the training from the effect of simply doing 30 minutes of memory tasks daily?

options.A: Training group versus Active Control group
options.B: Training group versus Passive Control group
options.C: Active Control group versus Passive Control group
options.D: Passive Control group's SD versus Training group's SD

explanation: Correct: Both groups do 30 minutes of memory tasks daily, differing mainly in whether the tasks are adaptive, so their difference (420 versus 460 ms) reflects adaptiveness. Why the others are wrong: B) The passive group did no tasks, so the difference mixes adaptiveness with task engagement. C) Neither group received adaptive training, so this comparison says nothing about adaptiveness. D) SDs describe spread, not the effect of the program.
trap: Using the passive control as the comparison, which cannot separate adaptive training from general task engagement.
